Airways.description: The small airways carry air from the larger bronchi into the acinus. The terminal bronchiole is the last airway that only conducts air, and respiratory bronchioles, whose walls have scattered alveoli, are where gas exchange begins. Their smooth muscle can narrow them, and club cells secrete a protective protein and surfactant components.
clinical: In asthma, the smooth muscle around the small airways contracts and narrows them. Inhaled β2-agonists relax this muscle and reopen the airway.
In smokers, inflammation starts in the respiratory bronchioles and destroys the alveoli around them, causing centrilobular emphysema.

Vessels.description: The pulmonary arterioles carry deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart alongside the airways to the capillaries that surround the alveoli. The capillaries form a dense sheet across the septa, and the pulmonary venules carry oxygenated blood back out along the edges of each lobule.
clinical: A blood clot lodged in a pulmonary artery blocks blood flow to part of the lung. That area is still ventilated but receives little blood, so oxygen uptake falls and the right side of the heart can be strained.
Chronic low oxygen, as in severe COPD, makes the small pulmonary arterioles narrow and thicken. Pressure rises in the lung circulation and can eventually strain the right side of the heart.

Alveoli.description: The alveoli are the small, thin-walled air sacs where gas exchange takes place. Their walls, the interalveolar septa, are lined mainly by flat type I cells that handle gas exchange, with cuboidal type II cells that make surfactant and alveolar macrophages that clear dust and microbes. Small pores of Kohn connect neighbouring alveoli.
clinical: Destruction of alveolar walls removes gas-exchange surface and leaves the lung overinflated. In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency the damage is panacinar, affecting the whole acinus and worst in the lower lobes.
In lobar pneumonia, exudate fills the alveoli, and the pores of Kohn let infection spread from one alveolus to the next.

Air–blood barrier.description: This is the thin wall between the air in an alveolus and the blood in a capillary. It is built from the flat type I cell, the fused basement membranes and the capillary endothelium, and is less than a micrometre thick, so gases diffuse across it quickly.
clinical: Scarring of the lung thickens the air–blood barrier, so gases cross it more slowly. People feel breathless, especially on exertion.
In acute respiratory distress syndrome, the barrier is injured and leaks, so fluid floods the alveoli and gas exchange fails.

Local specimen covers.description: These are removable openings cut into the walls of the air spaces so you can look inside. They are a viewing aid, not a natural gap in the lung.

Cell specimen covers.description: These are removable caps over the cytoplasm of some cells. Hiding a cap shows the whole, uncut nucleus inside that cell. They are a viewing aid, not a real anatomical structure.

parts.description: The terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway, a tube under 1 mm across at the end of the bronchiolar tree. Its lining is simple cuboidal epithelium of ciliated cells and club cells, and its wall has a complete ring of smooth muscle but no cartilage or glands. No alveoli open from it, and the airways beyond it, starting with the respiratory bronchioles, form the acinus where gas exchange takes place.

Respiratory bronchioles are the transitional airways of the acinus, lying between the terminal bronchioles and the alveolar ducts. Their wall is cuboidal epithelium interrupted by scattered alveoli that open directly into the lumen, so gas exchange begins here. In a section, look for a small airway with alveolar openings in its wall. Centriacinar emphysema, typical of smokers, is centred on this zone.

Bronchiolar smooth muscle is the layer of smooth muscle in the walls of the terminal and respiratory bronchioles, arranged as a continuous spiral sheet. Because bronchioles have no cartilage to hold them open, this muscle sets their calibre (inner width), and when it contracts the airway narrows, as in the bronchoconstriction of asthma. In a section, it shows as a band of elongated smooth muscle nuclei encircling a small airway that has no cartilage plates.

The pulmonary arterioles are the small branches of the pulmonary artery that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle into the lung. They run beside the bronchioles inside the bronchovascular bundles, a sheath of connective tissue shared with the airway, and branch into the capillaries of the alveolar septa. Their walls are thin, with only a modest layer of smooth muscle, because the pulmonary circulation runs at low pressure. In a section, look for a thin-walled vessel lying next to a bronchiole.

The pulmonary venules are the smallest veins of the lung. They collect oxygenated blood from the alveolar capillaries at the edges of each lobule and carry it on into the pulmonary veins, which return it to the left atrium. Unlike the arterioles, which run with the airways, venules lie in the interlobular septa, the connective tissue partitions between lobules. In a section, look for a thin-walled, blood-filled vessel in a septum, away from any airway.

The alveolar capillaries are the tiny blood vessels that form a dense network within the alveolar septa, and they are where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Each capillary is lined by endothelium, and it lies so close to the alveolar epithelium that the two share a fused basal lamina in places. In a section, look for narrow channels packed with red blood cells, with flattened endothelial nuclei along their walls.

The interalveolar septa of the alveolar ducts are the thin walls separating neighbouring alveoli around each duct. The alveolar duct is the short passage linking respiratory bronchioles to alveolar sacs, and its wall is made of these septa, with the mouths of the alveoli opening into it. Each septum is lined on both faces by alveolar epithelium and holds a dense capillary network, a few fibroblasts and fine elastic fibres. In a section, look for thin walls around a duct, with alveolar mouths between them.

The interalveolar septa of the alveolar sacs are the thin partitions between the neighbouring alveoli that cluster around each sac, the terminal air chamber of the acinus. Each septum is shared by two adjacent alveoli and contains capillaries with a few elastic and collagen fibres. Its two surfaces are lined by type I and type II pneumocytes. In a section, the sac septa look like thin, wavy walls dividing rounded alveolar profiles.

Pores of Kohn are small, round openings in the interalveolar septa that connect neighbouring alveoli. They allow collateral ventilation, meaning air can reach an alveolus by a side route when its own airway is blocked, and they let alveolar macrophages move from one air space to another. In a section, a pore shows as a small gap in an otherwise continuous septum.

Type II pneumocytes, or type II alveolar cells, are the cuboidal cells that lie among the flat type I cells, mainly at the corners where alveolar septa meet. They make and secrete pulmonary surfactant, a lipid and protein film that lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli from collapsing at the end of each breath. They also act as stem cells, dividing to replace damaged type I and type II cells. In a section, look for plump, cuboidal cells at septal corners.

Alveolar macrophages, or dust cells, are large phagocytic cells that lie free within the air spaces, mostly on the alveolar surface. They develop from blood monocytes, and they engulf and digest inhaled dust, bacteria and debris, a process called phagocytosis. In smokers, their cytoplasm often holds dark carbon pigment, which helps identify them. In a section, look for large, rounded cells in the alveolar lumen with granular cytoplasm.

Club (Clara) cells are the non-ciliated secretory cells of the bronchioles, lying among the ciliated cells of the lining. Their apex is dome-shaped and bulges into the lumen, and they secrete club cell secretory protein (CC10) and contribute to surfactant. They also break down inhaled toxins using cytochrome P450 enzymes, and act as stem cells that renew the bronchiolar epithelium. In a section, look for cells with a rounded apex and no cilia.

Alveolar duct smooth muscle consists of thin bundles of smooth muscle cells in the free edges of the septa, arranged around the openings (mouths) of the alveoli in an alveolar duct. In a section, each bundle appears as a small, rounded knob projecting into the duct. Together with elastic fibres, it helps set the calibre of the duct.

Type I pneumocytes, or type I alveolar cells, are the very thin, flat cells that line most of the alveolar surface and are the main site of gas exchange. Their cytoplasm is so thin across most of the cell that it is hard to see, except around the flattened nucleus, which bulges into the air space. Their flat shape keeps the distance for gas diffusion short. In a section, they are recognised mainly by their flattened nuclei.

Club cell nuclei are the nuclei of club (Clara) cells, the non-ciliated secretory cells lining the bronchioles. They are round to oval and sit towards the base of each cell, beneath the dome-shaped apex that bulges into the airway lumen. In a section, look for round nuclei low in the bronchiolar lining, among the ciliated cells.

Type II nuclei are the nuclei of type II pneumocytes, the cuboidal alveolar cells that make surfactant. Because these cells sit at the corners where alveolar septa meet, their nuclei are round rather than flattened, unlike the nuclei of type I cells. In a section, look for round nuclei in the corners of the septa, away from the thin, flattened walls of the alveoli.

Type II lamellar bodies are membrane-bound storage granules in the cytoplasm of type II pneumocytes, each made of many concentric layers of membrane. They hold the phospholipids and proteins that make up pulmonary surfactant, and they are released by exocytosis onto the alveolar surface, where they unravel into a film that reduces surface tension. They are seen only with an electron microscope, where they look like dense, layered bodies.

Macrophage nuclei are the nuclei of alveolar macrophages, the phagocytic dust cells that lie free in the air spaces. They are often indented or lobed, and sit within cells whose cytoplasm may contain dark dust particles. In a section, they can be told apart from the flattened nuclei of type I cells and the round nuclei of type II cells by their irregular outline and their position in the air space.

Type I nuclei are the flattened, oval nuclei of the type I pneumocytes that line the alveoli. Because these cells are so thin, the nucleus bulges into the air space and is the most visible part of the cell in a section. Their flattened outline is what distinguishes them from the round nuclei of type II cells.

The type I lining is the air-facing side of the air-blood barrier, formed by the extremely thin cytoplasm of type I pneumocytes that lines most of the alveolar surface. Its thinness lets oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse quickly between the alveolar air and the capillary blood. Neighbouring type I cells are joined by tight junctions, which seal the air space against fluid leakage. Its air-facing surface is coated by surfactant, the film that keeps the alveolus open.

The fused basal lamina is the shared sheet of basement membrane in the air-blood barrier, formed where the basal laminae of the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium lie against each other and merge. This membrane is made mainly of type IV collagen and laminin, and it gives the thin barrier its mechanical strength while still allowing gases to diffuse. It is seen only with an electron microscope, as a dense band that is thinnest where the two membranes fuse.

The capillary endothelium is the single layer of very thin, flattened endothelial cells that lines the alveolar capillary on the blood side of the barrier. These cells are joined by tight junctions and their cytoplasm is extremely thin, so gases pass through them easily. Inside the lumen, red blood cells carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin away from the barrier, which keeps the oxygen gradient steep.

The respiratory alveolar wall is the thin wall of the alveoli that open directly off a respiratory bronchiole. It is made of shared interalveolar septa, each lined on both faces by type I and type II pneumocytes and carrying a dense capillary network. Because air reaches these alveoli straight from the bronchiole, this is the first place gas exchange occurs in the acinus.

The duct alveolar wall is the wall of the alveoli that open off an alveolar duct, the short passage linking respiratory bronchioles to alveolar sacs. Between neighbouring alveolar mouths the wall is a thin septum, lined by type I and type II pneumocytes, and its free edge carries bundles of smooth muscle. In a section, it appears as a row of alveolar openings separated by thin septa, with small knobs of smooth muscle at their rims.

The sac alveolar wall is the wall of the alveoli that open onto an alveolar sac, the most distal air space in the acinus. Its alveoli are separated by thin shared septa, so the wall forms a honeycomb of small air spaces, with each septum carrying capillaries that meet the air. Lying at the far end of the airway tree, this wall marks the outer limit of the gas-exchange zone.

Type I cell cytoplasm is the cytoplasm of type I pneumocytes, the flat cells lining the alveoli. Across most of the cell it is extraordinarily thin, forming the air-facing lining of the alveolar wall, while the area around the nucleus is thicker and holds most of the cell's organelles. Because it is so thin, the sheet is hard to resolve in ordinary sections and is best seen with an electron microscope.

Type II cell cytoplasm is the cytoplasm of type II pneumocytes, the cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant. It is packed with lamellar bodies, the storage granules that release surfactant, and it contains rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria that support protein and surfactant production. In electron micrographs this dense, granular cytoplasm is what separates type II cells from the flat type I cells.

Club cell cytoplasm is the cytoplasm of club (Clara) cells, the non-ciliated secretory cells of the bronchioles. The dome-shaped apex contains secretory granules that release club cell secretory protein, and the cytoplasm is rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum carrying cytochrome P450 enzymes that detoxify inhaled chemicals. This apical dome is the part of the cell that bulges into the bronchiolar lumen.
